newsitem.title: JORDAN: Wheat to be Iraq's biggest purchase under UN deal.
newsitem.headline: Wheat to be Iraq's biggest purchase under UN deal.

text.p: Iraq's Minister of Trade Mohammed Mehdi Saleh on Sunday said wheat was the main component of two million tonnes of commodities it will buy under an six-month $2 billion U.N. oil-for-food deal.

"Our imports under the memorandum are around two million tonnes, which will ensure the operation of Umm Qasr and Aqaba port," Saleh told Jordanian businessmen in a meeting on the mechanism of the U.N. deal allowing Iraq to sell oil worth $2 billion over six months to pay for food and medicine.
He said wheat imports would make up the largest share of the oil-for-food deals, followed by rice, sugar, vegetable oils, detergents and soaps.
Saleh said Iraq would be importing 1.2 million tonnes of wheat, 340,000 tonnes of rice and 300,000 tonnes of sugar over the six-month period. A small 20,000-tonne allocation was set for tea.

Some of the proceeds of the $2 billion deal will be allocated to the U.N. compensation fund and its personnel, leaving Iraq $1.3 billion of the total sales to spend on humanitarian needs over six months.

Saleh said the oil-for-food deals totalling $1.35 billion over six months would have covered no more than one month's food imports before 1990, when the U.N. imposed economic sanctions after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait.
Iraqi imports before the Gulf crisis were in excess of $20 billion annually, including deferred payments and protocol accords, Saleh said.
Oil revenues alone in 1989 stood at $16.6 billion, Saleh said, adding that Iraq's losses as a result of the oil exports freeze have exceeded $120 billion over the six-year embargo.
Drugs and pharmaceuticals were allocated $220 million under the U.N. deal, followed by $170 million for vegetable oils and detergents and soaps, he added.
Saleh said $50 million was set aside for electricity generation equipment, while $40 million was allocated to agricultural supplies, including pesticides.
The U.N. deal also set aside small amounts for water purification chemicals and plastic bags for wheat packing, Saleh said, without giving figures.
Saleh stressed Iraq would purchase directly from world grain suppliers to help reduce costs and also to dispel any U.S. suspicions of collecting commissions by dealing with agents.

"There will be enormous difficulties not only in offering tenders through intemediary companies...but also the commodity that is imported via an intermediary company undoubtedly will have an extra cost," Saleh said.
"As a result of the competition, buying from the main source is necessary to reduce costs," Saleh added.

Saleh cited French grain supplier Drefyus as an example of a company that would be rewarded by being directly contacted in tenders once they are announced. This preferential treatment would apply to all firms that maintained sales to Iraq during the six-year embargo, he added.
He did not give a date when tenders under the oil-for-food deals would be announced, saying they were linked to the start of oil sales and collection of the proceeds.
